title: Rafael Mouallem Rosa
text:
Rafael Mouallem Rosa
I am a researcher at Inria, in the Statify team in Grenoble, France, working on Bayesian inference.
My current research centers on the Sources of Uncertainty (SoU) framework, which introduces confidence as an additional dimension of Bayesian inference, enabling the selective probabilistic treatment of different sources of uncertainty within a model. I explore its applications to statistical learning and macroeconometrics.
Before joining Inria, I completed a Ph.D. in Economics, working on decision theory, and later worked in financial markets as a quantitative portfolio manager. Across these experiences, a common theme has been uncertainty: the axiomatic study of choices under uncertainty, confronting uncertainty in financial markets, and modelling uncertainty in Bayesian statistical learning.

title: Rafael Mouallem Rosa
text:
I am a postdoctoral researcher at Inria working on Bayesian inference, model uncertainty, and statistical learning.
My current research develops the Sources of Uncertainty framework, an extension of Bayesian inference that allows researchers to model different degrees of confidence across components of a probabilistic model. This perspective connects ideas from decision theory, generalized Bayes, variational inference, and modern machine learning.
A central goal of my work is to develop Bayesian methods that remain useful when model uncertainty is not just a technical detail, but a core part of the problem. Recent applications include sparse Bayesian learning, global-local shrinkage methods, and self-pruning Bayesian neural networks.
Before joining Inria, I completed a Ph.D. in Economics, working on decision theory, and later worked in financial markets as a quantitative portfolio manager. This background shapes my interest in statistical methods for high-dimensional, uncertain, and decision-relevant environments.

title: Research
text:
My research focuses on Bayesian inference, model uncertainty, and statistical learning.
The central question in my current work is how Bayesian inference should be modified when the researcher has different degrees of confidence in different components of a probabilistic model. This question connects decision theory, generalized Bayes, variational inference, and modern machine learning.


I develop the Sources of Uncertainty framework, which extends Bayesian inference by assigning confidence parameters to different components of a probabilistic model.
The framework separates two ideas that are usually intertwined:

the informativeness of a prior;
the confidence assigned to the source of uncertainty represented by that prior.

This provides an additional modelling tool for controlling posterior concentration and regularisation.



Building on the Sources of Uncertainty framework, I study sparsity-inducing Bayesian methods based on global-local prior structures.
This leads to SoU-SGL, a sparse global-local estimator designed to recover sparse representations rather than merely shrink parameters toward zero.



I am also interested in Bayesian deep learning, especially methods that allow neural networks to adapt their effective architecture to the data.
Recent work applies the SoU framework to Bayesian neural networks, where it induces self-pruning and can lead to compact architectures without sacrificing predictive performance.

title: Research
text:
The Sources of Uncertainty (SoU) framework extends Bayesian inference by allowing researchers to express different levels of confidence in distinct sources of uncertainty within a model. This enables a selective probabilistic treatment of model components, controlling how uncertainty associated with each component is retained and propagated. As a particular case, some components can retain the standard Bayesian treatment while others approach optimization, with empirical Bayes and profiling emerging as limiting cases.
Confidence operates through a mechanism distinct from prior informativeness, providing a complementary modelling tool that can be tuned to shape the posterior. This introduces an additional degree of freedom in Bayesian model design.


In macroeconometrics, I develop SoU-BVARs, which allow confidence in estimated relationships between macroeconomic variables to adapt as new data become available. Confidence is assigned to blocks of autoregressive coefficients and learned sequentially from predictive evidence. Unlike adjustments to prior informativeness, this mechanism allows stronger regularization to coexist with greater posterior uncertainty about these relationships.
I evaluate the approach in a U.S. macroeconomic forecasting exercise across six BVAR specifications, combining Minnesota and Normal-Gamma shrinkage priors with constant covariance, stochastic volatility, and stochastic volatility with Student-t innovations. Adaptive source confidence improves average point and probabilistic forecast accuracy across all six specifications, outperforming both conventional Bayesian inference and a comparable approach that adapts prior informativeness.



In sparse Bayesian learning, I develop SoU-SGL, which uses selective probabilistic treatment to induce sparsity in global-local models. By assigning low confidence to local shrinkage scales, the method moves their treatment toward optimization while preserving Bayesian inference for the remaining components—an “optimize structure, infer parameters” approach.
I apply this mechanism to Bayesian neural networks through SoU-RHS, combining it with regularized horseshoe shrinkage to recover compact CNN architectures. The recovered architectures show stable size and layer-wise structure across starting widths and pruning thresholds, suggesting that the method identifies compact structures adapted to the data. They are substantially smaller than those obtained with deterministic structured-sparsity methods, while generally achieving higher accuracy, consistently lower negative log-likelihood, and better calibration in most settings.
